                                         Figure 1. Conventional navigation methods typically prioritize reaching a target location but do not account for constraints affecting
                                         manipulation feasibility. Left: Position A prioritizes proximity but is obstructed by chairs, preventing stable execution. Middle: Position
                                         B places the robot in a spacious and stable area for operation but beyond its effective reach. Right: Our approach, leveraging navigation
                                         affordance grounding, identifies Position C as the optimal stance, ensuring both reachability and task feasibility.

Figure 3. (a) Robot arms used in MoMa-Kitchen. The end-effectors of the Panda, Flexiv, Elephant, Realman and xArm6 robots are
grippers, while the end-effector of the UR5e is a suction cup. (b) Object categories utilized in MoMa-Kitchen. Each category consists
of multiple object instances. Rigid and articulated objects serve as manipulation targets, while obstacle objects are strategically placed
around the target to enhance scene complexity. (c) Examples of affordance maps in MoMa-Kitchen. Discrete affordance values are
first collected (left) by moving the mobile manipulator and allowing it to interact with the target. Gaussian interpolation is then applied to
obtain a smooth affordance map (right).

NAG uses the robot’s relevant information and the visu-                        Following standard practices in affordance grounding, we
ally aligned global point cloud to interact with the refer-                    utilize the mean squared error (MSE) loss as the primary ob-
ence floor, generating a robot-specific affordance predic-                     jective function to align the model’s predictions Pout with
tion for optimal positioning. As illustrated in Fig. 4(b),                     the ground truth affordance labels Plabel . In our exper-
NAG takes as input the feature-enhanced global point cloud                     iments, we observed that zero-valued elements constitute
P̄global from VAM, the floor point cloud Pf loor , and the                     a large proportion of the ground truth floor affordance la-
robot-related information RI . To extract features from the                    bels, leading to an imbalance between zero-valued elements
point cloud data, PointNet++ processes P̄global and Pf loor ,                  and those with non-zero values. To address this issue, we
yielding feature representations Fpcg and Fpcf , respec-                       apply a weighted mask to perform a weighted average on
tively. These features are then tokenized using a multi-                       the MSE loss (Weighted MSE). The Weighted MSE loss is
layer perceptron (MLP) in preparation for multi-head cross-                    computed by adjusting the weight for zero-valued elements

ing tasks; VoteNet and H3DNet, both originally designed                its larger parameter count. Consequently, within the same
for 3D object detection, are suited for adaptation to naviga-          training duration, H3DNet demonstrates the weakest per-
tion affordance grounding on our benchmark. By leverag-                formance. These findings suggest that a lightweight model
ing these models, we aim to establish strong baselines and             capable of fine-grained feature prediction may achieve su-
gain insights into how existing point cloud techniques per-            perior results on our MoMa-Kitchen benchmark.
form when applied to this new challenge.

levels: scenes, configurations, and episodes. Here, we pro-             tailed configuration of our simulation setup is specified be-
vide a detailed description of each level.                              low:

2.1. Evaluation Metrics
                                                                          SIM with higher values indicating better structural align-
In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the                 ment. Unlike PCC, which evaluates overall pattern
evaluation metrics used in our study. To comprehensively                  trends, SIM focuses on the overlap of affordance regions,
evaluate our method, we adopt five metrics: Root Mean                     making it particularly effective for assessing spatial align-
Squared Error (RMSE), Logarithmic Mean Squared Error                      ment. In our study, SIM ensures that predicted affor-
(logMSE), Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC), Cosine                   dance maps accurately capture the structural properties
Similarity (SIM), and Continuous Intersection over Union                  of ground truth.
(cIoU). Below, we describe each metric, its calculation for-
mula, and its relevance to our task.                                    2.2. Training Details
• RMSE: RMSE measures the numerical alignment be-                       To ensure a fair comparison, we train our model and all
  tween predicted and ground truth values. It penalizes                 baseline methods under consistent settings. The implemen-
  larger errors through squared differences, as defined be-             tations for both our methods and the baselines are developed


                                                                   14
using PyTorch. All models are trained on a single NVIDIA             regression components while retaining the remaining mod-
A100 GPU with a batch size of 64 for 6 epochs, complet-              ules to focus on navigation affordance grounding, enabling
ing the entire process in approximately 8 hours. We utilize          the network to predict affordance maps instead of object de-
the Adam optimizer [26] with betas configured as 0.9 and             tection outcomes.
0.999. The learning rate is initialized at 8e-4 and follows a
cosine decay schedule.                                               3. Additional Experimental Results
